title: Harbour at Dusk
tagline: The museum paid millions for a painting from 1890. The paint is younger than the lighthouse in it.

setting.place: Kestrel Museum of Art, conservation lab

briefing: Elise Varga, who died in 1898, painted the sea like nobody else. Last year the Kestrel Museum bought her 'Harbour at Dusk' for a record price.
This spring the museum's new scientist tested a speck of paint from the edge. The result made the director sit down.

Every painting has a paper trail, called its provenance: who owned it, when, and what they wrote about it. Somewhere in this one, the real painting stopped and a copy began. Find where, and you'll find who.
rules: Elise Varga painted the original 'Harbour at Dusk' before her death in 1898.
The documents below are genuine unless the evidence shows otherwise.

suspects.name: Felicity Dane
suspects.description: Inherited the painting from her grandfather, who bought it in 1962. Sold it in 2019.
suspects.motive: Needed money for her failing hotel.
suspects.statement: It hung in Grandpa's dining room my whole life. I sold the real thing, I'd swear to it.

suspects.name: Marcus Vell
suspects.description: Bought it from Felicity in 2019 and sold it to the museum in 2024. Trained as a painter before he became a dealer.
suspects.motive: Bought for a modest price and sold for a record one.
suspects.statement: I bought it, I had it cleaned, I sold it. I'm a dealer, not a magician.

suspects.name: Dr. Orla Quist
suspects.description: Wrote the book on Varga. Signed the certificate saying the painting was genuine.
suspects.motive: Her reputation, and her fee, depend on finding 'lost' Vargas.
suspects.statement: I judged it by eye and by style, as experts always have. It looked exactly right.

suspects.name: Tobias Wren
suspects.description: Cleaned the painting for Marcus in 2023. Has a studio full of paints and old canvases.
suspects.motive: Could paint a copy better than anyone.
suspects.statement: I clean pictures. I wrote down exactly what came through my door.

suspects.name: Nadia Bloom
suspects.description: Pushed the museum to buy the painting. Now the scandal is hers.
suspects.motive: Would have liked a famous acquisition on her record.
suspects.statement: I trusted the certificate and the dealer. I never touched the painting before it arrived here.

evidence.title: Paint analysis
evidence.source: Kestrel Museum conservation lab, this spring
body: Pigments found: lead white, ultramarine, and also titanium white and phthalocyanine blue throughout the whole picture, not just in a repaired patch.
Reference table from the lab's handbook: titanium white first sold to artists in 1921. Phthalocyanine blue first sold in 1935.

evidence.title: Grey Point lighthouse
body: The museum painting clearly shows a tall white lighthouse on the point.
Leaflet: “Grey Point lighthouse was built in 1949. Before that the point was bare rock.”

evidence.title: The paper trail
body: Each document records the painting's size, height × width.

rows: “Harbour at dusk, fishing boats, the bare point beyond.” Bought by Arthur Dane.
Photo of the Dane dining room, for a magazine
Looks about the size of the sideboard mirror beside it, 40 × 50 cm
The bare point is visible. No lighthouse.
Sale receipt, Felicity Dane to Marcus Vell
Restorer's condition report, on arrival from Marcus Vell
“Light grime. Lighthouse on the point is crisp.”
Certificate of authenticity, Dr. Orla Quist
Sale, Marcus Vell to Kestrel Museum

evidence.title: X-ray and canvas
body: The canvas is machine-woven and stamped on the back, under the frame: CANVASCO · PRIMED LINEN · BATCH 2016-114.

evidence.title: Marcus Vell's bank record
body: March 2020: payment received from a private collector in Geneva, reference “VARGA – HARBOUR – 40x50”.

evidence.title: Dr. Quist's appointment diary
body: One viewing of the painting, two hours, at Marcus Vell's gallery. No paint tests requested. Fee paid by Marcus Vell: her standard fee.

questions.prompt: What is the earliest year the museum's painting could have been painted?
questions.explanation: The pigments mean after 1935, but the picture also shows Grey Point lighthouse, built in 1949. It can't be earlier than 1949, half a century after Varga died.

questions.prompt: What size was the real 'Harbour at Dusk'?
questions.explanation: The 1962 catalogue, the 2015 photo and the 2019 receipt all record 40 × 50 cm, and the earlier records describe the bare point with no lighthouse.

questions.prompt: Between which two documents was the real painting swapped for the copy?

options.text: Between the 1962 catalogue and the 2015 photo
Between the 2019 receipt and the 2023 restorer's report
Between the 2023 report and the 2024 certificate

questions.explanation: In 2019 Felicity sold a 40 × 50 cm painting. By 2023, when it arrived at the restorer's from Marcus, it was 46 × 61 cm with a lighthouse.

questions.prompt: Who had the painting between those two documents?
questions.explanation: Marcus bought it in 2019 and sent it to the restorer in 2023. Felicity had already sold it, and Tobias, Orla and Nadia only saw it after it was 46 × 61 cm.

questions.prompt: What does the canvas stamp add?

options.text: The canvas was made in 2016 or later, so the copy was painted recently, after the 2015 photo, which fits a swap after 2019

questions.explanation: Batch 2016-114 dates the canvas to 2016 or later. The copy was painted recently, not in the 1950s.

The swap happened while Marcus owned the painting. He trained as a painter, and in March 2020 he sold a 40 × 50 cm 'Varga harbour', the real one, to a collector in Geneva. Then he sold his own copy to the museum.

solution.summary: Marcus Vell bought the real 'Harbour at Dusk' from Felicity Dane in 2019 for a modest price. He quietly sold it to a private collector in Geneva in 2020, then used his old painter's training to make a copy on a modern canvas. Working from the present-day harbour, he painted in the lighthouse that wasn't there in Varga's time, and made it a little larger to look grander. He had it cleaned to give it a history, got Dr. Quist's certificate after a two-hour look, and sold the fake to the museum. He was paid twice for one painting.

chain.step: The museum's painting has 1921 and 1935 pigments throughout and shows a lighthouse built in 1949: it's a fake.
The real one was 40 × 50 cm with a bare point (1962, 2015, 2019). The fake is 46 × 61 cm.
The size changes between the 2019 receipt and the 2023 restorer's report, while Marcus owned it.
The canvas is from 2016 or later.
Marcus sold a 40 × 50 cm Varga harbour to Geneva in 2020.

eliminations.why: The 2019 receipt, signed by both, records the true 40 × 50 cm size; she sold the real painting.
Careless, not a forger: she saw it once, in 2024, already 46 × 61 cm.
His 2023 report records it arriving at 46 × 61 cm with the lighthouse, so it was already the fake.
Only received it in 2024, long after the swap.

playtest.solvePath: Players often date the fake using only the pigments (1935) and then find the lighthouse. The paper-trail table is where the case is won: spotting the size change. Most solve it in 30 to 40 minutes.
pitfalls: Some suspected Tobias, the restorer, because he has the skills. His own arrival report clears him, which is why it's included.
Players asked whether Felicity sold a fake in 2019. The receipt size and the bare point in the 2015 photo show she had the real one.
revisions: Added the lighthouse so the earliest date is a clean 1949, not just 'after 1935'.
Put sizes on every document so the swap can be pinned between two specific records.
Added the canvas batch number to show the fake is modern and not a 1950s copy that slipped in earlier.
